unit-alg-t2-03.title: Topic 2 · 2-3 Factored Form of a Quadratic Function
unit-alg-t2-03.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-3: Factored Form of a Quadratic Function

cards.def:
**y = a(x − p)(x − q), where p and q are the zeros of the function.**
• Each zero is a value that makes the function equal to 0.
• The x-intercepts of the graph are exactly p and q.
cards.hint: Factored form's whole job is making the zeros visible instantly.

cards.def:
**A value z where f(z) = 0 — where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.**
• Also called an x-intercept, or a root of the equation.
• A quadratic function can have zero, one, or two real zeros.
cards.hint: Zero of the FUNCTION, x-intercept of the GRAPH — same thing, two names.

cards.def:
**If a product of factors equals 0, at least one of the factors must be 0.**
• For two factors: if ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0 (or both).
• This is the only reason factoring lets you solve an equation — without it, factoring would just be rewriting, not solving.
cards.hint: The ONLY way a product can be 0 is if one of the things being multiplied already is.

cards.def:
**Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b — those numbers become the constants in each factor.**
• x² + bx + c factors as (x + m)(x + n) when m·n = c and m + n = b.
• Check your factoring by multiplying back out with the Distributive Property.
cards.hint: Multiply to the LAST number, add to the MIDDLE number.

cards.def:
**Find two numbers that multiply to a·c and add to b, then split the middle term and factor by grouping.**
• The target product is a times c, not just c, since a is no longer 1.
• Once split, group the four terms in pairs and pull out the common factor from each pair.
cards.hint: The target number to multiply to is a·c, not c — that's the one thing that changes from the a = 1 case.

cards.def:
**Each factor (x − p) becomes 0 exactly when x = p — that's why the zeros and the factors match up.**
• y = (x + 4)(x − 2) has zeros at x = −4 and x = 2 — not 4 and −2.
• The sign inside each factor is the OPPOSITE of the zero it produces.
cards.hint: Same sign-flip trap as vertex form's h — the number IN the factor is the opposite of the zero.

cards.def:
**Set the equation equal to 0, factor the expression, then apply the Zero Product Property to each factor.**
• Every quadratic equation can be rearranged into the form (something) = 0 first.
• Once factored, each factor set equal to 0 gives one solution.
cards.hint: Always get to "= 0" BEFORE you factor — factoring a sum that isn't 0 doesn't help you solve anything.

cards.def:
**A quadratic function's sign can only flip at its zeros — test one point in each interval between them to find where it's positive or negative.**
• Two zeros divide the number line into three intervals.
• The sign stays constant across an entire interval; it never changes in the middle of one.
cards.hint: Pick ANY test point in an interval — the answer will be the same no matter which one, as long as it's in that interval.

cards.term: Writing factored form from x-intercepts and a point
cards.def:
**Substitute the two zeros for p and q, then use a third point to solve for a.**
• y = a(x − p)(x − q) starts with p and q known from the intercepts.
• The extra point pins down a, the only unknown left.
cards.hint: Same overall method as vertex form — fill in what you know, solve for what's left.

cards.term: Example: matching zeros to a graph
cards.def:
**y = (x − 5)(x + 1) has zeros at x = 5 and x = −1.**
• The graph crosses the x-axis at exactly those two points.
• Between the zeros the graph is negative (since a > 0 and it dips below the axis); outside them it's positive.
cards.hint: y = (x − 5)(x + 1) expands to x² − 4x − 5, vertex at (2, −9) — same parabola, factored form just names the crossing points.

cards.term: Application: when does a projectile land
cards.def:
**A projectile hits the ground when its height function equals 0 — solve by factoring for the zeros, then keep only the positive one.**
• Time can't be negative, so a negative zero is always thrown out in these problems.
• The positive zero is the answer: how long until it lands.
cards.hint: Factoring gives you two zeros; the context throws one of them away.

questions.q: What does the Zero Product Property state?
opts: If a product of factors equals 0, at least one factor must be 0
Any number multiplied by 0 equals that number
The product of two zeros is always 0
A quadratic function always has exactly two zeros
questions.hint: It's about what a product being 0 tells you about its factors.
steps: The Zero Product Property is a statement about products that equal 0.
It says that if ab = 0, then a must be 0, or b must be 0 (or both).
So the correct statement is: if a product of factors equals 0, at least one factor must be 0.

ex.main: **If a product of factors equals 0, at least one factor must be 0.** This one fact is the entire reason factoring can solve an equation.

questions.q: What is the factored form of x² + 9x + 20?
questions.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to 20 and add to 9.
steps: Look for two numbers whose product is 20 (the last term) and whose sum is 9 (the middle coefficient).
4 and 5 multiply to 20 and add to 9.
So the factored form is (x + 4)(x + 5).

ex.main: **(x + 4)(x + 5).** Check it: 4 × 5 = 20 and 4 + 5 = 9 — both conditions match.

questions.q: What is the factored form of x² − 5x − 14?
questions.hint: The two numbers multiply to −14 and add to −5.
steps: Find two numbers whose product is −14 and whose sum is −5.
−7 and 2 multiply to −14 and add to −5.
So the factored form is (x − 7)(x + 2).

ex.main: **(x − 7)(x + 2).** −7 and 2: product −14, sum −5 — both check out.

questions.q: What is the factored form of 2x² + x − 15?
questions.hint: With a leading coefficient of 2, the target product is 2 × −15, not just −15.
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to 2 × (−15) = −30 and add to 1: those are 6 and −5.
Split the middle term: 2x² + 6x − 5x − 15, then group: 2x(x + 3) − 5(x + 3).
Factor out the common (x + 3): (x + 3)(2x − 5).

ex.main: **(x + 3)(2x − 5).** When a isn't 1, the target product is a·c — here 2 × −15 = −30 — not just c.

questions.q: The graph of y = x² − 4x − 5 has zeros at x = 5 and x = −1. What are the factors of x² − 4x − 5?
questions.hint: Each factor's sign is the OPPOSITE of its zero.
steps: A zero of x = 5 comes from a factor of (x − 5), since x − 5 = 0 exactly when x = 5.
A zero of x = −1 comes from a factor of (x + 1), since x + 1 = 0 exactly when x = −1.
So the factors are (x − 5)(x + 1).

ex.main: **(x − 5)(x + 1).** The zero x = −1 comes from (x + 1), not (x − 1) — the sign inside the factor is always the opposite of the zero it produces.

questions.q: What are the zeros of the function y = (x + 3)(x − 8)?
questions.hint: Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.
steps: Set the first factor to 0: x + 3 = 0, so x = −3.
Set the second factor to 0: x − 8 = 0, so x = 8.
The zeros are x = −3 and x = 8.

ex.main: **x = −3 and x = 8.** Each factor, set to 0 and solved, hands you one zero directly — that's the entire value of factored form.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 3x = 40?
questions.hint: Move everything to one side first — factoring only works on an expression equal to 0.
steps: Rewrite the equation so one side is 0: x² + 3x − 40 = 0.
Factor: find two numbers multiplying to −40 and adding to 3 — those are 8 and −5. So (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0.
By the Zero Product Property: x + 8 = 0 gives x = −8, and x − 5 = 0 gives x = 5.

ex.main: **x = −8 and x = 5.** The equation had to be rearranged to "= 0" before factoring could solve it at all.

questions.q: A ball is thrown from a platform. Its height is modeled by h(x) = −16x² + 64x + 80, where x is time in seconds. When does the ball hit the ground?
questions.hint: The ball hits the ground when height equals 0 — factor and solve, then throw out the answer that can't be a real time.
steps: The ball hits the ground when h(x) = 0: −16x² + 64x + 80 = 0.
Factor out −16 first: −16(x² − 4x − 5) = 0, then factor the trinomial: −16(x − 5)(x + 1) = 0.
The zeros are x = 5 and x = −1. Since time can't be negative, only x = 5 makes sense — the ball hits the ground after 5 seconds.

ex.main: **5 seconds.** Factoring hands you both zeros; the real-world context is what tells you to discard the negative one.

questions.q: On which interval(s) is the function y = x² − 4x − 5 positive?
questions.hint: Find the zeros first, then test a point in each of the three resulting intervals.
steps: Factor to find the zeros: y = (x − 5)(x + 1), so the zeros are x = 5 and x = −1.
These two zeros split the number line into three intervals: x < −1, −1 < x < 5, and x > 5.
Testing a point in each — x = −2 gives a positive value, x = 0 gives a negative value, x = 6 gives a positive value — shows the function is positive on x < −1 and x > 5.

ex.main: **x < −1 and x > 5.** A quadratic function's sign can only flip AT its zeros, so testing one point per interval is enough to know the whole interval.

questions.q: A parabola has x-intercepts (2, 0) and (6, 0), and passes through (4, −8). What is its equation in factored form?
questions.hint: Substitute the intercepts for p and q, then use the third point to solve for a.
steps: Substitute the intercepts: y = a(x − 2)(x − 6).
Solve: a = 2. The equation is y = 2(x − 2)(x − 6).

questions.q: A parabola has x-intercepts at 0 and 5, and passes through (2, −6). What is its equation in factored form?
questions.hint: An intercept of 0 makes one factor just x, not (x − 0) written out.
steps: An x-intercept at 0 means one factor is (x − 0), which simplifies to just x. So y = a·x(x − 5).
Substitute the point (2, −6): −6 = a(2)(2 − 5) = a(2)(−3) = −6a.
Solve: a = 1. The equation is y = x(x − 5).

ex.main: **y = x(x − 5).** a came out to exactly 1, so it doesn't even need to be written — a nice check that the arithmetic worked out clean.

questions.q: A student says the zeros of y = (x − 2)(x + 7) are −2 and 7. Is the student correct?
questions.hint: Set each factor to 0 and solve — don't just read the numbers as they appear.
steps: Set the first factor to 0: x − 2 = 0, so x = 2, not −2.
Set the second factor to 0: x + 7 = 0, so x = −7, not 7.
The correct zeros are 2 and −7 — the student read both signs backwards.

ex.main: **No — the zeros are 2 and −7.** Reading a factor's number as the zero directly, without flipping its sign, is exactly the error the student made.

questions.q: What is the factored form of x² − 2x − 24?
questions.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to −24 and add to −2.
steps: Find two numbers whose product is −24 and whose sum is −2.
−6 and 4 multiply to −24 and add to −2.
So the factored form is (x − 6)(x + 4).

questions.q: What is the factored form of 3x² − 2x − 8?
questions.hint: The target product is 3 × −8, not just −8.
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to 3 × (−8) = −24 and add to −2: those are −6 and 4.
Split the middle term: 3x² − 6x + 4x − 8, then group: 3x(x − 2) + 4(x − 2).
Factor out the common (x − 2): (x − 2)(3x + 4).

questions.q: What is another name for a zero of a quadratic function?
questions.hint: It's the point where the graph crosses or touches one particular axis.
steps: A zero is a value of x where the function's output is 0.
On a graph, that's exactly where the graph crosses (or touches) the x-axis.
So a zero is also called an x-intercept.

ex.main: **An x-intercept.** "Zero of the function" and "x-intercept of the graph" describe the exact same point, from two different angles.

questions.q: On which interval(s) is the function y = (x − 3)(x − 9) negative?
opts: There is no interval where it's negative
questions.hint: Test a point between the zeros, and one outside them, to compare.
steps: The zeros are x = 3 and x = 9, which split the number line into x < 3, 3 < x < 9, and x > 9.
Testing x = 6 (between the zeros): (6 − 3)(6 − 9) = (3)(−3) = −9, which is negative.
Testing x = 0 and x = 10 (outside the zeros) both give positive results, so the function is negative only on 3 < x < 9.

ex.main: **3 < x < 9.** Between two zeros of an upward-opening parabola is exactly where the graph dips below the x-axis.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 7x = 30?
questions.hint: Rearrange to "= 0" first, then factor.
steps: Rewrite as x² + 7x − 30 = 0.
Find two numbers multiplying to −30 and adding to 7: those are 10 and −3. So (x + 10)(x − 3) = 0.
By the Zero Product Property: x = −10 or x = 3.

questions.q: Which equation is written in factored form?
questions.hint: Factored form has two separate binomials multiplied together.
steps: Factored form has the shape y = a(x − p)(x − q) — two separate linear factors multiplied.
y = 4x² − 8x − 12 is standard form (fully expanded). y = 4(x − 1)² − 16 is vertex form (one squared binomial).
Only y = 4(x − 3)(x + 1) has the two-separate-factors shape of factored form.

ex.main: **y = 4(x − 3)(x + 1).** Two distinct linear factors multiplied — that's the signature shape of factored form.

questions.q: A rectangular garden's area, in square feet, is modeled by A(x) = (x + 4)(x − 6), where x is a length in feet. For what values of x does this model represent a real garden with positive area?
questions.hint: A length has to be positive AND the area has to be positive — check both.
steps: The zeros of A(x) are x = −4 and x = 6, splitting the intervals into x < −4, −4 < x < 6, and x > 6.
Testing shows A(x) is positive on x < −4 and x > 6, and negative on −4 < x < 6.
Since x also represents a length, it must be positive too — combining both conditions leaves only x > 6 as physically meaningful.

ex.main: **x > 6.** The algebra alone allows x < −4, but a negative length isn't a real garden — the context rules that interval out.

questions.q: What is the factored form of x² + 7x − 30?
questions.hint: Find two numbers multiplying to −30 and adding to 7.
steps: Find two numbers whose product is −30 and whose sum is 7.
−3 and 10 multiply to −30 and add to 7.
So the factored form is (x − 3)(x + 10).
